lede: A very short preface. Greene sets out what the book is about (our universe may not be the only one) and how to read it: which parts can be skipped and who the notes are for.

points.h: Everyday experience deceives
points.body:
The opening line sets the tone: by the twenty-first century it is settled that **everyday experience is an unreliable guide to the true nature of reality**.

His explanation is evolutionary. Hunting on the savanna, there was no survival advantage in being able to calculate the quantum behavior of electrons. But as our brains grew, we built instruments to extend our senses and invented a method for "detecting and expressing pattern", namely mathematics, and only then could we see past appearances.

points.h: The next upheaval: maybe more than one universe
points.body: The behavior of space, time, matter and energy has already gone far beyond anything anyone has seen with their own eyes. Following these discoveries further may bring the next upheaval in understanding: **our universe may not be the only universe.** This book explores that possibility.

points.h: How to read this book
points.body:
- It assumes no background in physics or mathematics, relying on metaphor, analogy and stories from the history of science
- Unlike his two earlier books (*The Elegant Universe* and *The Fabric of the Cosmos*), it **does not lay the groundwork systematically first** for relativity and quantum mechanics; it explains them "as needed"
- The last few pages of many chapters go deeper; a brief summary comes first, and newcomers can skip straight past
- The notes are for readers with mathematical training; newcomers can ignore them entirely

For reading together, this means: for the harder part at the end of each chapter, read his short summary first and come back to work through the details if you are interested.

points.h: A small Easter egg in the acknowledgments
points.body: The acknowledgments name many people who turn up in later chapters: Linde (inflation), Susskind (the landscape and holography), Steinhardt (the cyclic universe), Maldacena (holographic duality), Tegmark (the mathematical universe), Vafa and Shing-Tung Yau (the shape of the extra dimensions). The last line thanks his wife and children for making this **the best of all possible universes**.

expressions.en: common experience is deceptive
expressions.zh: Everyday experience is deceptive. The starting point of the book, and the opening stance of all of Greene's books.

expressions.en: a systematic method for detecting and expressing pattern—mathematics
expressions.zh: Mathematics is defined as "a systematic method for detecting and expressing pattern", not as formulas or calculation. This definition becomes important in Chapter 10, on mathematical reality.

expressions.en: a landscape of ideas that peak by valley stretches from the everyday to the wholly unfamiliar
expressions.zh: A landscape of ideas running, peak by valley, from the everyday to the wholly unfamiliar. The word *landscape* will later become the term for string theory's "Landscape Multiverse"; here it is planted early.

expressions.en: the will to persevere
expressions.zh: The only prerequisite is "the will to persevere". Very Greene-style encouragement.

expressions.en: making this the best of all possible universes
expressions.zh: A twist on Leibniz's famous phrase "the best of all possible worlds", swapping *worlds* for *universes* to match the book's theme.

questions: Greene says everyday experience deceives us, and that we see through appearances by means of mathematics. Could mathematics itself also be a kind of "appearance"?
He chose not to lay the groundwork first, explaining things as he goes. Does that make the book easier or harder for you to read?

lede: The map of the whole book. Greene starts with two facing mirrors in his childhood bedroom, then lays out the route ahead: nine kinds of parallel universe, and the branch of physics each one comes from.

points.h: A childhood between two mirrors
points.body:
In Greene's childhood room, the mirror on the wardrobe door faced a mirror on the wall, reflecting an endless line of himself. Knowing that light travels at a finite speed, he imagined light bouncing back and forth between the mirrors, each image pushing the next; he even fantasized that somewhere far down the line a "rebel me" refused to follow along and rewrote all the reality after it.

The images of course had no minds of their own, but this childhood daydream matches an increasingly important theme in modern science: **there may be other worlds beyond the one we know.**

points.h: The word "universe" has changed
points.body:
"Universe" used to mean "everything". Now its meaning depends on context:
- Sometimes it still means absolutely everything
- Sometimes only the part we could, in principle, get access to
- Sometimes one of many realms separated from each other (partly or completely, temporarily or permanently), with ours just one member

He uses parallel worlds, parallel universes and *multiverse* as synonyms. As for what exactly counts as "a universe", he borrows US Supreme Court Justice Potter Stewart's line about defining pornography: **I know it when I see it.** Whether we call them parallel universes is only a matter of language. What matters is whether what we have always called "the universe" might be just a small piece of a larger, stranger, mostly hidden reality.

points.h: Quantum mechanics: the first parallel worlds
points.body:
In the 1950s, parallel worlds first emerged from quantum mechanics. Quantum mechanics predicts only the **probabilities** of various outcomes, but there is a less discussed puzzle: why does only one of them actually happen? For over a century physicists have had no consensus on this.

The most startling answer is: **every possible outcome happens, each in its own universe.** In each universe there is a you who sees one outcome and believes your reality is the only one. "There's no such thing as a road untraveled." This is the **Many Worlds interpretation**, still controversial today (Chapter 8).

Greene also lists the parallel-world stories he loved growing up: *The Wizard of Oz*, *It's a Wonderful Life*, the *Star Trek* episode "The City on the Edge of Forever", Borges's "The Garden of Forking Paths", *Sliding Doors* and *Run Lola Run*.

points.h: Route map of the book
points.body:
- **Chapter 2, the Quilted Multiverse**: if space is infinite, there must be copies of you far away
- **Chapter 3, the Inflationary Multiverse**: inflation may keep blowing out universe after universe in distant places, without end
- **Chapter 4**: an introduction to string theory and where it stands
- **Chapter 5, the Brane and Cyclic Multiverses**: we are a "slice of bread" in higher-dimensional space; colliding branes set off new big bangs, giving universes that are parallel **in time**
- **Chapter 6, the Landscape Multiverse**: the extra dimensions have a vast number of possible shapes, each realized somewhere; also the dark energy that fills space
- **Chapter 7**: whether parallel universes count as science
- **Chapter 8, the Quantum Multiverse** (Many Worlds)
- **Chapter 9, the Holographic Multiverse**: everything we experience may be a holographic projection of processes on a distant surface; Greene thinks this is the strangest of all
- **Chapter 10, the Simulated and Ultimate Multiverses**: can we make universes? Are we living in a simulation? And "every possible universe exists"

points.h: His stance: not selling, just following the chain of reasoning
points.body:
**No experiment or observation has confirmed any kind of parallel universe.** Greene says he did not write the book to convince you; he himself is not convinced, and no one should be convinced of anything without hard data.

What he finds interesting is that many developments in physics, pushed far enough, run into some kind of parallel universe. Physicists are not going out with nets to catch them; these ideas **emerge unbidden** from the mathematics of theories developed to explain ordinary data.

points.h: Does a multiverse make humanity smaller?
points.body: Some feel that if there are many universes, humanity's place is marginalized. Greene disagrees: meaning should not be measured by numbers. What makes being human, and doing science, interesting to him is that we can **cross vast distances through analytical thought**, perhaps even beyond the boundaries of our universe. The understanding gained from one lonely corner of a cold, dark cosmos is the mark of our "having been there".

expressions.en: The whole shebang.
expressions.zh: Slang for "the whole lot, everything". Following a serious definition with a bit of slang is a rhythm Greene often uses.

expressions.en: I know it when I see it.
expressions.zh: Justice Potter Stewart's famous line from a 1964 obscenity case. Greene uses it to sidestep the hard problem of defining what counts as a universe, both funny and candid.

expressions.en: there’s no such thing as a road untraveled
expressions.zh: A quiet nod to Robert Frost's "The Road Not Taken": in Many Worlds, every road is taken by someone.

expressions.en: With its hegemony diminished, “universe” has given way to other terms
expressions.zh: The "hegemony" of the word "universe" has weakened. A change in a word's meaning described as a shift in power.

expressions.en: multiverse nets in their hands
expressions.zh: Physicists are not walking around with multiverse butterfly nets, waiting to snare any passing theory. A vivid self-defense.

expressions.en: emerge unbidden from the mathematics
expressions.zh: *Unbidden* means uninvited. It is the key to the book's argument: parallel universes are not invented, they are deduced.

expressions.en: the catoptric musings of my boyhood
expressions.zh: *Catoptric* means "relating to mirrors or reflection", a very obscure word. Using a learned term for childhood musings in front of a mirror brings the chapter back to the two mirrors of its opening.

expressions.en: the inky black stillness of a cold and forbidding cosmos
expressions.zh: Ink-black, still, cold and forbidding: the lyrical closing line of the chapter.

questions: Greene says whether we call them parallel universes is "only a matter of language". What do you think is the difference between a region we can never reach and one that does not exist?
Many Worlds says every possibility happens in some universe. If that is true, do your choices still mean anything?
He thinks human worth lies in the depth of our understanding, not in how rare we are in the cosmos. Do you agree?

lede: The simplest kind of parallel universe: if space is infinitely large, and the particles in each observable region can be arranged in only finitely many ways, then far away there must be infinitely many worlds exactly like ours, including a you reading this sentence.

points.h: Opening: another you, far away
points.body:
If the universe is infinite, then far away there is a galaxy exactly like the Milky Way, an Earth exactly like ours and a you exactly like you, reading this book right now and imagining a distant you. Not just one, but **infinitely many**: some reading this line in step with you, some who skipped ahead, some who put the book down for a snack, some with such a foul temper you would not want to meet them in a dark alley.

Nor will you meet them: they are so far away that light has not had time to cross the distance since the big bang.

points.h: The father of the big bang: a priest and Einstein
points.body:
At the 1927 Solvay conference, the Belgian priest and physicist **Georges Lemaître** told Einstein that general relativity implied the universe had expanded from a "primeval atom". Einstein replied: **"Your mathematics is correct, but your physics is abominable."**

Alexander Friedmann had found expanding solutions in 1921; Einstein first said he had made a mistake, then retracted. Einstein refused to be "mathematics' pawn" and was convinced the universe was eternal and unchanging. Six years later at Mount Wilson, after hearing Lemaître's talk, he stood up and called it "the most beautiful and satisfactory explanation of creation to which I have ever listened".

points.h: General relativity: space itself carries gravity
points.body:
Newton's law of gravity is very accurate (NASA still uses it), but it cannot answer **how** the Sun, across 150 million kilometers of vacuum, holds on to the Earth. In the *Principia* Newton left the question "to the consideration of the reader". For over two hundred years readers just read on. Einstein did not.

His answer: there is something in the vacuum after all, namely **space itself**. The analogy is a metal table: when it is flat, a marble rolls in a straight line; if fire warps the table, the marble follows a curved path. The Sun curves the space (more precisely, spacetime) around it, guiding the Earth around it.

Confirmations: the orbit of Mercury (when Einstein calculated it he had heart palpitations for hours), the bending of starlight during the 1919 eclipse (the *New York Times* headline: "Lights All Askew in the Heavens"), the Cassini probe, and the **GPS** in your phone.
> The key point in a footnote: for objects like the Earth and Sun, what dominates is actually **the warping of time**. A clock on the ground runs slower than one on top of the Empire State Building; objects "want" to move toward where time runs slower, so things fall.

points.h: The cosmological principle: the universe is like a cup of tea
points.body:
To use general relativity on the whole universe, Einstein first simplified: the **cosmological principle**, that on the largest scales the universe is uniform. Like a cup of tea: microscopically there are water molecules, tea polyphenols and gaps, but macroscopically it is a uniform brown.

Observations support this, provided the scale is at least 100 million light-years: put one box 100 million light-years across here and another a billion light-years away, and the average number of galaxies, amount of matter and temperature are almost indistinguishable. "**If you've seen one, you've pretty much seen them all.**"

This assumption reduces the ten tangled equations of general relativity to one: it cuts the Gordian knot.

points.h: The universe cannot stand still, hence the cosmological constant
points.body:
The simplified equation told Einstein that the density of the universe cannot stay constant: it must expand or contract. Think of a baseball: gravity pulls in only one direction, and with no opposing force, the ball cannot hang in mid-air. Neither can the universe.

Greene uses a **tax form** to explain Einstein's fix. The "form" of general relativity has three lines: one for the geometry of spacetime (gravity), one for the distribution of matter (the source of gravity), and a third for **the energy contained in space itself**. Einstein originally left the third line blank, which amounts to entering zero. To get a static universe, he entered a precisely chosen positive number there: a uniform positive energy produces **repulsive gravity**, exactly balancing the attraction of matter. This is the **cosmological constant**.

Greene stresses that this change was "small and entirely reasonable", not a reckless tampering with the equations.

points.h: Hubble: the universe is expanding
points.body:
In 1929 Hubble, using the largest telescope of the day, found that distant galaxies are all moving away from us: the universe is expanding. Einstein's reason for the cosmological constant evaporated; had he not been swayed by the prejudice of a static universe, he could have predicted the expansion more than a decade earlier.

But Greene leaves a hint: the story of the cosmological constant is far from over.

points.h: Possible shapes of the universe
points.body:
The cosmological principle narrows the possible shapes of space to a few uniform ones. Think in two-dimensional analogies:
- **Positive curvature**: the surface of a billiard ball (a sphere), finite
- **Zero curvature**: an endlessly extending tabletop (infinite), or a **torus** like the Pac-Man screen where you leave on the left and come back on the right (finite)
- **Negative curvature**: an endlessly extending Pringles chip (infinite)

A mirror analogy: in a positively curved mirror you bulge outward, in a negatively curved one you shrink inward, and with zero curvature you are undistorted.

points.h: The measurement: flat
points.body:
The curvature depends on the density of matter and energy in the universe. The **critical density** is about six hydrogen atoms per cubic meter, the equivalent of a single drop of rain in a volume the size of the Earth.

When astronomers count up the stars and the inferred matter, they get only 27% of the critical density. In the late 1990s they also found a uniform, non-luminous energy filling space, **dark energy**, making up about 73%. The two add up to exactly 100%: **the spatial curvature of the universe is zero**.

So the universe is either the infinite tabletop or the finite Pac-Man screen. The cosmological constant Einstein abandoned may have returned in the form of dark energy (Chapter 6).

points.h: Finite or infinite, and why it matters
points.body:
If the universe is finite, light might go all the way around and come back, letting us see repeated images of the same galaxy (the two mirrors again). None have been found, which means that even if it is finite, it is big enough to pass for infinite.

The age of the universe (about 13.7 billion years) is unaffected. But the picture differs: a finite universe, run backward, shrinks to a tiny point; **an infinite universe is infinite at every moment**, just denser the earlier you go. Half of infinity is still infinity.

Greene says physicists privately tend to favor infinite, partly just because historically people did not bother analyzing the mathematically more complicated torus. And finite versus infinite is by no means just an academic question.

points.h: The quilt: patches of universe that never touch
points.body:
Step one: the **cosmic horizon**. Because light travels at a finite speed, light from things too far away has not yet reached us. Because space is expanding, the farthest we can see is about 41 billion light-years, not 13.7 billion. Regions beyond the horizon have never had any contact with us and evolve independently.

Picture space as a **quilt** of round patches, each patch a cosmic horizon. Patches far enough apart are completely independent. If space is infinite, there are infinitely many patches.

points.h: The fly's protest: the possibilities are finite
points.body:
Step two: within each patch, there are **only finitely many** ways to arrange the particles.

Greene writes a dialogue with a fly in a bedroom. You say: the room is so big you could be in infinitely many positions. The fly objects: two positions a billionth of a centimeter apart are indistinguishable to me, so they are not two places.

Quantum mechanics turns the fly's intuition into law: the **uncertainty principle**. The more precisely you measure position, the less precisely you know speed; higher resolution requires higher-energy probes, and perfect resolution would need infinite energy. A photography analogy: with a fast shutter the position is clear but you cannot see the speed; with a slow shutter there is motion blur and the position is unclear. So "changes too small to be measured, even in principle, are not changes at all".

Add that a region can hold only so much energy (pack in too much and it becomes a black hole), and the number of particles is finite too. A single horizon has about **10 to the power 10^122** distinct particle arrangements: enormous, but finite.

points.h: Inevitable repetition: infinitely many yous
points.body:
Two everyday examples set this up: Imelda has 500 dresses and 1,000 pairs of shoes, 500,000 combinations, so within about 1,400 years she must repeat an outfit; Randy shuffles enough decks of cards that some order must repeat. **Infinitely many instances + finitely many configurations = infinite repetition.**

Likewise, infinitely many patches with finitely many arrangements means every arrangement (ours included) is repeated infinitely many times. This is the **Quilted Multiverse**.

Greene is candid about his position: **a physical system is fully determined by the arrangement of its particles**, human minds and bodies included, with no additional soul or "vital spirit". So a distant you with the same arrangement is you, and there is no telling which one is "real".

Distance estimates: an exact copy of the whole observable universe appears about once every 10 to the 10^122 meters; a copy of just the few light-years around the Sun, about once every 10 to the 10^100 meters. Near copies are even more common: every choice you have made or turned down plays out in some patch. But most patches have no life at all.

points.h: Can it be refuted?
points.body:
If the conclusion seems too outlandish, you can challenge the premises:
- Beyond the horizon it is all empty? Theoretically very awkward, not credible
- The laws of physics change far away? The next chapter shows that the conclusion holds even if the laws vary
- **The universe is finite?** This is the strongest objection: a small finite universe has room for only a few patches

But the next chapter's **inflationary cosmology** makes an infinite universe almost inevitable, and brings with it another, stranger kind of parallel world.

expressions.en: Your mathematics is correct, but your physics is abominable.
expressions.zh: Einstein's verdict on Lemaître. The irony is that the one whose physics later proved "abominable" was Einstein himself.

expressions.en: Einstein refused to be mathematics’ pawn.
expressions.zh: Einstein refused to be a pawn of the mathematics. This time intuition overrode mathematics and was wrong, a contrast with the book's stance of following the math.

expressions.en: he gibingly left the question “to the consideration of the reader,”
expressions.zh: Newton mockingly left the question "to the consideration of the reader". The follow-up, *those who read this challenge simply read on*, is a nice touch: the readers read it, and simply kept reading.

expressions.en: The emptiness of empty space seemingly left everyone empty-handed.
expressions.zh: A pun on *empty* used three times, then the turn: there is something in space after all, namely space itself.

expressions.en: LIGHTS ALL ASKEW IN THE HEAVENS, MEN OF SCIENCE MORE OR LESS AGOG
expressions.zh: A real 1919 *New York Times* headline. *Agog* means eagerly excited or open-mouthed.

expressions.en: It’s the art of knowing what to ignore.
expressions.zh: Theoretical physics as the art of knowing what to leave out. It could describe a lot of creative work.

expressions.en: if you’ve seen one 100-million-light-year chunk of the cosmos, you’ve pretty much seen them all
expressions.zh: A play on the saying *if you've seen one, you've seen them all*, stretched comically to a scale of 100 million light-years.

expressions.en: cuts the Gordian knot
expressions.zh: To cut the Gordian knot is to solve a tangled problem with one bold stroke, after the story of Alexander the Great slicing through the knot. Here it is the cosmological principle reducing ten equations to one.

expressions.en: Only a wise fly would claim to be able to tell the difference.
expressions.zh: A pun: *wise fly* sounds like *wise guy* (a smart aleck).

expressions.en: the number of discernibly distinct positions and speeds available to a well-funded fly
expressions.zh: A "well-funded fly": a joke about research funding slipped into a thought experiment.

expressions.en: a less than felicitous disposition
expressions.zh: A very genteel way of saying "a nasty temper", followed immediately by *someone you'd rather not meet in a dark alley*.

expressions.en: Changes that are too small to be measured, even in principle, are not changes at all.
expressions.zh: The key sentence of the chapter's argument.

questions: Greene believes a person is fully determined by the arrangement of particles. If you disagree (for example, if you think consciousness is more than that), does the Quilted Multiverse conclusion still hold?
Einstein trusted intuition over mathematics and was wrong; Greene's book follows the mathematics all the way. When should we trust mathematics, and when intuition?

"Infinitely many tries + finitely many possibilities = inevitable repetition." Does this reasoning hold in music too? With finitely many combinations of notes and rhythms, must melodies eventually repeat?
If there really were someone far away exactly like you, would you feel that person is "you"?

lede: Why is the cosmic microwave background almost the same temperature everywhere? Inflation provides the answer, and along the way implies that inflation may never stop in distant regions, blowing out "bubble universe" after bubble universe, each of which is infinite when seen from inside.

points.h: The afterglow of the big bang: a neglected discovery
points.body:
Switch off the Sun and sweep away all the galaxies, and space is still not dark at microwave wavelengths: everywhere is the **cosmic microwave background radiation** left over from the big bang.

About 370,000 years after the big bang, the universe cooled to 3,000 K, electrons and protons combined into atoms, and photons that had been bounced around by charged particles could suddenly fly freely. The expansion of space has since stretched and cooled them to about 2.7 K today.

**George Gamow**'s team (Alpher and Herman) predicted it in the late 1940s, but their papers were ignored. In the 1960s, Dicke and Peebles at Princeton derived it again and were about to build an instrument to look for it; thirty miles away at Bell Labs, Penzias and Wilson had an antenna with a hiss they could not get rid of however they adjusted it, and assumed their equipment was faulty. A chain of chance conversations brought the two groups together, and they agreed to publish simultaneously in the *Astrophysical Journal*: Princeton on the theory, Bell Labs reporting the measurement in the most cautious terms with not a word about cosmology. The Nobel Prize went to Penzias and Wilson; Gamow's team was only slowly recognized years later.

A bit of trivia: about 1% of the snow on an old television with no signal comes from big bang photons.

points.h: The horizon problem: why places that never met are equally hot
points.body:
The microwave background has almost exactly the same temperature in every direction. When you shake hands, the temperature difference between two hands evens out quickly, but only through **contact**. Yet two points at opposite ends of the sky never had a chance to exchange any information in the standard big bang theory, like two tribes who have never been in touch speaking the same language and owning the same books. This is the **horizon problem**.

Greene says he was at first "puzzled by the puzzle": in the early universe everything was close together, so how could there not have been time for contact? The answer: the speed of light limits how fast objects move **through space**, not how fast **space itself** expands. Early on, space expanded so quickly that regions were pulled apart faster than light and could not reach thermal equilibrium.

points.h: Inflation: slow first, then violent, and gravity can repel
points.body:
In 1979 **Alan Guth** proposed inflation, later refined by Linde, Steinhardt and Albrecht. The idea: first there was enough time for all regions to reach the same temperature, then a brief, extremely violent burst of accelerated expansion pulled them to the vast separations we see today.

The question is what could drive such expansion. Newton would find it absurd: gravity only attracts. But in general relativity, gravity comes not only from mass but also from **pressure**. Positive pressure contributes attraction; **negative pressure contributes repulsive gravity**. Einstein used it to build a static universe (the wrong use); inflationary theory uses it to make the universe explode.

points.h: Quantum fields and the inflaton
points.body:
A **field** cannot be seen or touched, but a magnet holding a paperclip from a distance is evidence of one. Faraday and Maxwell established the electromagnetic field, and in the second half of the twentieth century it was combined with quantum mechanics into **quantum field theory**.

Why does a uniform field have negative pressure? The champagne analogy: pop the cork and carbon dioxide pushes outward (positive pressure). Now fill the bottle with a uniform field instead: when you pull the cork, you feel it **pulling back in**, because the extra space in the bottle is also filled with the field and also carries energy, and you have to supply that energy with your effort. That is negative pressure. The cosmological constant works the same way.

The hypothetical field that drives inflation is called the **inflaton**, dropping the second *i* in keeping with names like electron and proton.

points.h: Cartman and the energy plateau
points.body:
Greene's analogy is the round **Eric Cartman** of *South Park* perched on a snowy mountain top: the value of the inflaton field sits on a gentle plateau high on its energy curve, full of energy and negative pressure, driving inflation; then it "rolls down the slope", the energy turns into particles, inflation ends and ordinary expansion takes over.

In a typical version, inflation enlarged space by a factor of about 10^30 in about 10^-35 seconds: a region the size of a pea was stretched larger than the entire observable universe, in far less than the blink of an eye. The tiny region that gave rise to our observable universe could reach a uniform temperature before it was stretched, and the horizon problem is solved.

points.h: Eternal inflation: the virus outruns the vaccine
points.body:
Inflation is a framework, not a specific theory. The most important version, developed by Vilenkin and Linde, says: **inflation is not a one-off event.**

Two details the Cartman analogy leaves out: the inflaton has a value at **every point in space**, and it is subject to **quantum jitters**. Picture a whole row of Cartmans on identical mountain tops, each shaken by random earthquakes: some roll down, some stay up.

The crucial point: regions still high up expand rapidly, producing more high-value regions; regions that roll down form a bubble. In most successful inflationary models, "breeding" outpaces "eradication", like a virus that spreads faster than it can be cleared, and **inflation never stops**.

points.h: A Swiss cheese universe
points.body:
The universe is like a huge, ever-expanding block of **Swiss cheese**: the cheese is the region where the inflaton is still high and inflation continues; the **holes** are regions where inflation has stopped, each one a **bubble universe**, ours among them.

Don't be fooled by the small word "bubble": each one is as vast as our universe. There are also models in which inflation eventually stops everywhere, but they are the exception.

points.h: From dismissed to mainstream
points.body:
In the 1980s Vilenkin went eagerly to MIT to tell Guth about eternal inflation, and halfway through **Guth fell asleep**. (Greene says this is not necessarily a bad sign: Guth is famous for dozing in seminars, has done so during Greene's own talks, and then opens his eyes midway to ask the sharpest question.) At the time people saw it as "speculation piled upon speculation".

Observations later changed everything. Inflation stretched **quantum jitters** from the microscopic to the macroscopic, like tiny writing on an uninflated balloon that becomes legible once it is blown up. This left temperature spots of one part in a hundred thousand in the microwave background. The COBE team first measured them, and Smoot and Mather won the 2006 Nobel Prize; WMAP and later measurements match inflation's predictions remarkably well.

We should all be grateful for these spots: slightly denser regions had slightly stronger gravity, drew in more matter, and snowballed into galaxies and stars.

points.h: Physics in other bubbles
points.body:
In the quilted universe the patches are broadly alike; the bubbles of the inflationary multiverse are **entirely separate**, and their properties may be completely different.

Imagine a bubble filled with a magnetic field a thousand times stronger than an MRI that can never be switched off: the fundamental laws are the same as ours, but experimental results and environments are very different. Our universe may have something similar: the standard model assumes we are immersed in a **Higgs field**, and particles gain mass from "friction" with it.

The Higgs field's energy curve may have several valleys, and in different bubbles it may settle into different valleys, giving different particle masses and force strengths. Make the electron a few times heavier, and electrons and protons merge into neutrons: no hydrogen, no stars, no us. **Same laws, different environments**: traveling between bubbles would be dangerous.

points.h: Infinity in a nutshell: bubbles are infinite from inside
points.body:
This section links the two kinds of multiverse. Hamlet says: "I could be bounded in a nutshell, and count myself a king of infinite space." A bubble universe looks finite in size from outside but is **infinite** from inside.

The reason is that time is defined differently. People inside a bubble keep time using **a quantity that changes uniformly** (today the average density of matter, like carbon-14 dating; early on, the value of the inflaton): points with the same inflaton value are "the same moment". An outside observer, Trixie, sees the bubble grow without limit over time; Norton, inside, joins up points by inflaton value into "all of space at one moment", and these curves extend without end.

**Endless time seen from outside appears inside as endless space at each moment.** So the infinite space Chapter 2 needed no longer has to be assumed: every bubble is infinite, and each contains a Quilted Multiverse.

points.h: Parallel parallel universes
points.body: Greene says he found the inflationary version more convincing from the start: it solves old problems like the horizon problem, and its predictions agree with observation. The picture that our best cosmological theory produces is that we live in one bubble of an inflationary multiverse, and each bubble contains countless quilted universes. Not just parallel universes, but **parallel parallel universes**.

expressions.en: a kayak stocked with a healthy assortment of chocolate and brandy
expressions.zh: In 1932 Gamow and his wife tried to kayak across the Black Sea to escape the Soviet Union, with "a healthy assortment of chocolate and brandy" on board. Driven back to shore by the weather, he talked his way out of trouble with a story about a failed scientific experiment at sea.

expressions.en: the cosmic monotony was interrupted by a pivotal turn of events
expressions.zh: The cosmic monotony broken by a pivotal turn: 370,000 years of murk written like the plot twist in a film.

expressions.en: I became puzzled by the puzzle
expressions.zh: The repetition gives the line rhythm and leads into the key point that the expansion of space is not limited by the speed of light.

expressions.en: galaxies don’t have jet engines
expressions.zh: Galaxies recede because space is stretching, not because they are moving under their own power: a one-line explanation.

expressions.en: there’s no sommelier uncorking the cosmos
expressions.zh: Nobody is uncorking the universe. This reins in the earlier champagne analogy and turns back to the real cosmos.

expressions.en: nearly round Eric Cartman—perched precariously on one of South Park’s snow-covered mountains
expressions.zh: First a ball, then "better to picture Cartman": a typical Greene escalation of the joke. *Perched precariously* means balanced in a risky spot.

expressions.en: The inflationary virus effectively resists eradication.
expressions.zh: An epidemic metaphor for why eternal inflation cannot be stopped.

expressions.en: the descriptive but diminutive-sounding “bubble universe”
expressions.zh: Vivid, but it makes them sound small. *Descriptive* and *diminutive* alliterate.

expressions.en: Guth is famous for nodding off during physics seminars—he’s caught a few winks during talks I’ve given
expressions.zh: *Nod off* and *catch a few winks* both mean to doze. Greene jokes at his own expense that Guth has slept through his talks too.

expressions.en: speculation piled upon speculation
expressions.zh: The verdict on eternal inflation at the time.

expressions.en: we should all be thankful for the blotches
expressions.zh: Without the uneven temperatures in the microwave background there would be no galaxies, and no us.

expressions.en: I could be bounded in a nutshell, and count myself a king of infinite space
expressions.zh: From Act 2 of *Hamlet*; Hawking's book title *The Universe in a Nutshell* comes from the same line. Greene uses it to capture a bubble that is finite outside and infinite inside.

expressions.en: not only parallel universes but parallel parallel universes
expressions.zh: Stacking the word conveys the nesting, layer within layer.

questions: The speed of light limits motion through space but not the expansion of space itself. Does this distinction strike you as a deep physical fact or as a kind of "loophole in the rules"?
If in other bubbles the electron has a different mass and there are no atoms, do they still count as "universes"? What gives us the right to call them that?
The same bubble is finite seen from outside and infinite seen from inside, depending on how "the same moment" is defined. Here time seems more fundamental than space. What do you make of that?
Gamow's team predicted the microwave background but did not win the Nobel Prize. In the history of science, which deserves more to be remembered: saying it first or measuring it first?

lede: A break from parallel universes for a "checkup" on string theory: where it came from, what it set out to solve, what it has achieved and what it still lacks. As a string theorist, Greene gives a fairly candid report card.

points.h: Einstein's unfinished dream of unification
points.body:
Einstein spent the last thirty years of his life fixated on a **unified field theory**: stitching gravity and electromagnetism into a single mathematical tapestry. He failed, partly because his focus was too narrow: he was dismissive of quantum mechanics and did not consider the strong and weak nuclear forces, which had just been discovered.

In the 1960s and 70s the tide turned: quantum field theory successfully described the electromagnetic, weak and strong forces. But applied to the fourth force, **gravity**, the mathematics broke down. In the mid-1980s **superstring theory** arrived; from the mid-1990s, refinements of its mathematics unexpectedly pushed it into the multiverse story.

points.h: Quantum field theory: unbeatable, but it can't handle gravity
points.body:
Two key features of quantum field theory: disturbances of a field come in discrete lumps, **particles**; and every field has **quantum jitters**. None of its predictions has ever been overturned by experiment, and its precision is astonishing.

But for the gravitational field, calculating the jitters produces infinite probabilities. Greene's analogy: you own an old house in San Francisco. The electromagnetic, strong and weak forces are "tenants"; however loud their parties, they never threaten the structure. But jitters in the gravitational field are **the house itself shaking**: an earthquake.

This conflict surfaces only in extreme conditions: things that are both very heavy and very small, like the center of a black hole or the big bang. The relevant scale is the **Planck length** (about 10^-33 centimeters), a hundred billion billion times smaller than the smallest scale experiments have probed.

points.h: String theory in one sentence
points.body:
Elementary particles used to be thought of as points with no internal structure. String theory says: zoom in to the Planck scale, and inside every particle is a tiny, vibrating **string of energy**. All strings are the same; they differ only in their **pattern of vibration**: the more frantic the vibration, the higher the energy and the greater the mass (E=mc²). Electrons, quarks and photons are the same kind of string "playing" different notes.

"In a nutshell, that's string theory."

points.h: Three highlights of string theory
points.body:
- **Particles grow out of the theory itself**: in quantum field theory you choose by hand which fields to include; in string theory every vibrational pattern is a particle
- **Gravity comes built in**: one vibrational pattern of the string has exactly the properties the quantum of the gravitational field should have, so gravity and quantum mechanics are reconciled
- **It continues a historical pattern**: successful new theories do not overthrow old ones but extend them into extreme conditions (Newton to relativity to quantum). When the string scale cannot be resolved, string theory reduces to general relativity and quantum field theory

points.h: Extra dimensions: the straw and the carpet
points.body:
Stranger still, string theory's mathematics requires **more dimensions** of space: 10 spacetime dimensions in all (9 of space plus time), and 11 in the later M-theory. Greene admits he cannot give a non-technical reason, and has never seen anyone else do so.

Dimensions don't go missing like car keys or socks, so where did the extra ones go? Two analogies:
- A **drinking straw** as tall as the Empire State Building: you see the vertical direction at a glance, but the circular direction around it is so small that from a distance it looks like a line
- A **carpet** covering the Utah salt flats: from a plane it looks like a two-dimensional surface; only up close do you notice the dimension of the pile

Around 1919 **Kaluza** and **Klein** had already proposed that with one extra curled-up dimension, gravity and electromagnetism could both be seen as ripples in space. Einstein hesitated for two years (sitting on Kaluza's paper in the meantime) and eventually became a supporter of hidden dimensions.

points.h: The biggest regret: it can't calculate particle properties
points.body:
Why does the electron have this mass, the up quark this charge? Quantum field theory can **never** answer that: these values are its inputs.

String theory held out hope: strings also vibrate in the extra dimensions, so **the shape of the extra dimensions** (a Calabi–Yau space) determines the vibrational patterns and hence the particle properties. Greene's doctoral thesis was an early attempt along these lines, and he later did a postdoc under Shing-Tung Yau.

The problem is there are too many shapes: at first just a few, then thousands ("that's what graduate students are for"), and now more than **all the grains of sand on all the beaches, by a long shot**. The mathematics has not picked out a unique shape, so on this point string theory **has so far done no better than quantum field theory**. Chapter 6 argues that in a multiverse, expecting the mathematics to pick out one shape may itself be a mistake.

points.h: How to test it? Indirect evidence
points.body:
Seeing strings directly would require an accelerator the size of the galaxy, consuming a thousand years of the world's electricity every second. So we can only look for evidence that "could just about be explained by conventional means, but is far more naturally explained by string theory": rather as you could suppose I type with my toes, but fingers are obviously more plausible.

Candidates:
- **Supersymmetric partner particles** (LHC)
- **Extra dimensions diluting gravity**: gravity leaks into the extra dimensions, which is why it is much weaker than the other forces; testable by measuring gravity below a micron
- **Missing energy**: collision debris flying off into the extra dimensions
- **Tiny black holes** (LHC)
- Gravitational waves from **cosmic strings**
- Signatures in the **microwave background**

The harsh part: a positive result would hardly **prove** string theory right, and a negative one would hardly **prove** it wrong.

points.h: Singularities, black hole entropy and contributions to mathematics
points.body:
- **Singularities**: general relativity breaks down where space is punctured. A point particle would fall into the hole, but a string has length and can wrap around and snag, so the equations still hold. Orbifold singularities, flop singularities (which Greene helped work on) and others have been tamed by string theory. But the singularities of black holes and the big bang remain unresolved
- **Black hole entropy**: string theory precisely calculated the black hole entropy that Bekenstein and Hawking proposed in the 1970s (Chapter 9)
- **Mathematics**: strings can wrap around cylindrical spaces (like a rubber band around a soda can), which led to the discovery that **two spaces with entirely different geometry can give the same physics** (mirror symmetry). This "hard problem to easy problem" dictionary helped mathematicians count how many spheres can fit inside a Calabi–Yau space. Whether or not string theory is right, it is already a powerful tool for mathematics

points.h: The report card
points.body:
Greene's summary table:
- Unifying gravity and quantum mechanics: **excellent** (essential)
- Unifying all forces: excellent (not essential)
- Incorporating past theories: excellent
- Explaining particle properties: **incomplete, no predictions**
- Experimental confirmation: **incomplete, no predictions** (the most important item)
- Resolving singularities: excellent, but black hole and big bang singularities still open
- Black hole entropy: excellent
- Contributions to mathematics: excellent

A theory in progress with remarkable achievements that has yet to pass the most important exam: experiment.

expressions.en: stitch all of nature’s forces into a single, coherent mathematical tapestry
expressions.zh: *Stitch* and *tapestry* are both images of needlework, echoing the quilt of Chapter 2.

expressions.en: the leitmotif of string unification
expressions.zh: A *leitmotif* is the recurring musical theme tied to a character or idea in Wagner's operas. All strings being identical is the leading theme of string unification. Since string theory is itself a musical metaphor, the word fits especially well.

expressions.en: In a nutshell, that’s string theory.
expressions.zh: The previous chapter quoted Hamlet's nutshell; here *in a nutshell* (in brief) doubles as a callback.

expressions.en: Dimensions of space don’t go missing like car keys or one member of your favorite pair of socks.
expressions.zh: Missing car keys and the lone sock from your favorite pair: a homely contrast to make the point that dimensions can't simply vanish.

expressions.en: but that’s what graduate students are for
expressions.zh: (Thousands of shapes to analyze) but that's what graduate students are for. Dry humor in the voice of an adviser.

expressions.en: more numerous than grains of sand on a beach. Every beach. Everywhere. By a long shot.
expressions.zh: A string of fragments, each one upping the stakes. *By a long shot* means by a wide margin.

expressions.en: could cope without blinking an eye
expressions.zh: Without hesitation. Quantum field theory will accept any electron mass you give it, which is exactly why it cannot explain the actual value.

expressions.en: you might theorize that I’m typing these words with my toes
expressions.zh: "You might theorize I type with my toes", but the more natural explanation (to which he can attest) is fingers. An illustration of how indirect evidence works.

expressions.en: much like a rubber band stretched around a can of soda
expressions.zh: A picture of a string wrapping around a space, something a point particle cannot do.

expressions.en: “We just don’t know what’s going on,”
expressions.zh: Situations about which Einstein, Bohr, Heisenberg, Wheeler and Feynman would all have said "we just don't know what's going on", yet string theory can describe them completely.

questions: Greene says successful new theories usually fold old ones in as special cases. Can you think of similar cases of "extending rather than overthrowing" in the history of music or art?
A positive result can't prove string theory right, and a negative one can't prove it wrong. Does such a theory still count as science?
Einstein held on to Kaluza's paper for two years before backing it. Is the hesitation of eminent figures a safeguard for science or an obstacle?
All particles as different vibrational patterns of the same string: what does this picture mean to someone who makes music?

lede: In the mid-1990s, string theory broke free of approximate calculations and found that besides strings there are "branes". Our universe may be a brane in higher-dimensional space, with other universes hovering a few millimeters away; branes colliding periodically could bring one new big bang after another.

points.h: The risk of approximation: a final exam problem
points.body:
Writing a final exam at Cornell late one hungry night, Greene casually tweaked a classic problem (a ladder sliding down a wall) by letting the ladder's density vary along its length. The next day, writing out the solution himself, he found that the original problem took half a page and the new one six.

**Textbook problems are deliberately designed to be solvable**; change them slightly and they become as hard as the real world. A physicist's skill is knowing which complications can be dropped. But approximation has risks: a detail irrelevant to one problem may be crucial to another. In the mid-1990s, string theorists discovered that their approximation methods had missed key physics.

points.h: Perturbation: the lottery example
points.body:
Ralph says: the chance of winning each week is one in a billion, so buying two weeks makes it two in a billion. Alice points out that this slightly overestimates: the case of winning both weeks is counted twice. Calculate the main contribution first, then refine with smaller corrections: this is the **perturbative approach**.

Particle collisions work the same way: first calculate "one collision", then two, three and so on, each extra step multiplying by a **coupling constant**. If the coupling constant is small, the corrections shrink quickly and the approximation is accurate; if it is large, the approximation fails.

String theory has a **string coupling constant**, which researchers long assumed was small. But what if it isn't?

points.h: Duality: the five string theories are one family
points.body:
In the 1980s it was found that string theory comes in **five versions** (Type I, Type IIA, Type IIB, Heterotic-O and Heterotic-E).

In spring 1995, **Edward Witten** shook the whole field: turn up the coupling constant of one string theory and it **morphs into another string theory with a small coupling constant**. A problem that is hard to calculate at strong coupling becomes easy on the dual side.

Greene's analogy: a picture that looks like Einstein up close and like Marilyn Monroe from afar. Looking only at the two extremes you would think they were two people, but it is the same picture. The five string theories are joined into one by a web of dualities, collectively called **M-theory**. This is known as the **second superstring revolution**.

points.h: Branes: more than strings
points.body:
Why only one-dimensional strings? Higher-dimensional objects (disks, blobs) were once thought to lead to mathematical contradictions. The new methods showed those contradictions were just **artifacts of approximation**.

So string theory came to include two-dimensional **membranes** (like Frisbees or flying carpets) and higher-dimensional "p-branes" (three-branes, four-branes and so on). Another stunning result: the number of space dimensions is not 9 but **10** (11 including time). When Witten announced these results at a 1995 conference at the University of Southern California, Greene remembers a room full of stunned faces.

points.h: The Brane Multiverse: slices in a loaf
points.body:
Branes can be very large, even infinite. A huge **three-brane** could fill the space we occupy, as water fills a fish tank.

But string theory has more space dimensions. So imagine that everything we take to be the whole universe (Orion, the Horsehead Nebula, the Milky Way, Andromeda...) lies on **one three-brane**, like a slice in a cosmic loaf of bread, with other slices, other universes, next to it. This is the **Brane Multiverse**.

Each brane follows the same fundamental laws, but the environment (field values, even the number of space dimensions) can differ. Which raises the question: if other universes hover right next door, like slices of rye bread side by side, why can't we see them?

points.h: Sticky branes, and gravity's tentacles
points.body:
Strings come in two kinds: **closed loops** and **open segments**. Joe Polchinski found that the endpoints of open strings **can only sit on branes**.

You and all ordinary matter are made of open strings, so you are stuck firmly to our brane: try to jump off our three-brane, try harder, and you are still here. The particles that carry the electromagnetic, strong and weak forces are open strings too, so **light cannot leave the brane either**, and we cannot see the neighboring universes.

Only the **graviton** is a closed string (spin 2): with no endpoints it can leave the brane and travel through the extra dimensions. That may explain why gravity is so weak: it **leaks away into other dimensions**.

This gives Chapter 4's experiments new meaning: if the extra dimensions are larger than thought (say 10^-4 centimeters), precision gravity experiments might detect them; missing energy or tiny black holes at the LHC could be evidence that **we live on a brane**.

points.h: The Cyclic Multiverse: parallel in time
points.body:
The other members of the previous multiverses are "over there", separated in space. The **Cyclic Multiverse** is different: its universes are arranged **in time**.

If our brane moves through the extra dimensions and hits a neighboring brane, the result would be extremely violent: high temperature, high density, particles spraying everywhere, very much like the moments just after the big bang. Steinhardt, Turok and others proposed on this basis that the big bang may have been the collision of two branes.

And colliding branes do not stick together; they **bounce apart**, gravity slows them, they approach and collide again, like two giant hands clapping over and over. A full cycle takes about **a trillion years**. Our universe is just the latest in a long series; earlier ones may have had intelligent life and cultures, long since obliterated, and everything we contribute will eventually be erased too.

points.h: An old problem for cyclic universes, and a new answer
points.body:
The cyclic view of the cosmos is ancient: day and night, the seasons, the cosmologies of many civilizations are cyclic. Friedmann proposed an oscillating universe in 1923. Its appeal lies in **sidestepping the question of how the universe began**: having your cake and eating it too.

In the 1950s Zanstra pointed out the fatal problem: **the second law of thermodynamics**. Entropy (disorder) only increases, just as a kitchen that is tidy in the morning is bound to be a mess by evening. Entropy builds up every cycle, so there cannot have been infinitely many cycles already.

Steinhardt's team responded: what cycles is **the distance between the branes**, while the branes themselves keep expanding. Entropy increases every cycle, but it is spread over ever larger branes, so the **entropy density** returns to its starting value each time.

points.h: A testable difference: primordial gravitational waves
points.body:
The cyclic model makes a prediction that differs from inflation: inflation violently disturbs spacetime and should leave significant **primordial gravitational waves**, imprinted on the microwave background; the cyclic model's brane collisions are gentler and **produce no** observable gravitational waves.

If the LHC finds evidence of a braneworld while primordial gravitational waves remain elusive, the Cyclic Multiverse would gain support. For now, the physics community is broadly aware of it and broadly skeptical.

points.h: Flux: 10^500 outfits
points.body:
Branes have another property: **flux**. Just as electrons produce electric fields and magnets produce magnetic fields, branes produce their own "field lines". Bousso, Polchinski and others realized that describing the extra dimensions requires specifying not only their shape and size but also **how branes wrap and how flux threads** through them.

Calabi–Yau spaces have many "holes" (like the inside of a beach ball or the hole of a donut). A rough count: each hole can carry 10 kinds of flux; one hole gives 10 options, two give 100, and some shapes have about 500 holes, giving about **10^500 forms** of the extra dimensions, vastly more than the number of particles in the observable universe.

More refined mathematics, far from picking out a unique answer, has brought an **abundance of possibilities**. Three reactions:
- Some think string theory has thereby lost its predictive power
- Some are optimistic: one day the missing principle will be found
- Radicals say: perhaps decades of failing to find a unique shape is itself telling us that **all the shapes are real**, each corresponding to a universe. That is the next chapter

expressions.en: This one took me six pages. I write big. But you get the point.
expressions.zh: Three short sentences, with just the right touch of self-mockery.

expressions.en: “Really, wise guy. What do you mean close?”
expressions.zh: Ralph's indignation at being corrected by Alice. In an earlier chapter the fly was a *wise fly*; here we get a real *wise guy* (a smart aleck).

expressions.en: Minus the smugness, Alice’s method is an example of what physicists call a perturbative approach.
expressions.zh: A quick dig at the character, then straight to the point. *Smugness* is self-satisfied superiority.

expressions.en: navigate beyond the shores of small couplings
expressions.zh: Calculation methods described as a voyage of exploration beyond familiar coastlines.

expressions.en: The morphing from Einstein to Monroe is amusing. The morphing of one string theory into another is transformative.
expressions.zh: *Amusing* and *transformative* are set in parallel: a party trick versus a revolution.

expressions.en: the rationale for excluding anything but strings was rickety
expressions.zh: The reason for allowing only strings was shaky. *Rickety* originally describes wobbly furniture.

expressions.en: slices of rye cozying up to their neighbors
expressions.zh: Parallel universes made homely: slices of bread nestling against each other. *Cozy up to* means to snuggle close.

expressions.en: Try to jump off our three-brane. Try again, harder. I suspect you’re still here.
expressions.zh: Greene addresses the reader directly, demonstrating an abstract conclusion with a physical action.

expressions.en: gravity’s tentacles
expressions.zh: A section heading: only gravity can reach beyond the brane.

expressions.en: the colliding cosmic tango
expressions.zh: Two branes advancing and retreating and colliding again and again, like dancers in a tango.

expressions.en: an attempt to have your cosmological cake and eat it too
expressions.zh: From the saying *you can't have your cake and eat it too*. The cyclic universe wants both an eternal cosmos and a big bang.

expressions.en: Kitchens, however ordered in the morning, have a way of becoming disordered by nightfall
expressions.zh: The most domestic statement of the second law of thermodynamics.

expressions.en: a feather in the Cyclic Multiverse’s cap
expressions.zh: *A feather in one's cap* is an achievement to be proud of.

expressions.en: Calabi-Yau spaces can clothe themselves with far more outfits than there are particles in the observable universe
expressions.zh: Echoes Imelda's dresses and shoes from Chapter 2: Calabi–Yau spaces have more outfits than the observable universe has particles.

expressions.en: Maybe, these radicals brazenly continue
expressions.zh: A run of sentences starting with *Maybe* mimics the radicals getting bolder as they go. *Brazenly* means shamelessly or boldly.

questions: We are "stuck" to the brane, and only gravity can leave. If that is true, could gravity be our only link to other universes?
In the cyclic universe, earlier universes may have had civilizations that were then completely erased. Does that make you feel a sense of futility, or rather of relief?
Greene says textbook problems are designed to be solvable. When you studied music theory, did you ever find that exercises went smoothly but real pieces got hard as soon as something changed?
Faced with 10^500 possibilities, which of the three attitudes (give up, wait, they are all real) do you lean toward?

lede: In 1998, supernova observations revealed that the expansion of the universe is accelerating: the discarded cosmological constant was back, and absurdly small. Theory cannot calculate it. Greene works his way through the anthropic principle, string theory's 10^500 shapes and eternal inflation, which together offer a highly controversial explanation. The turning point of the book.

points.h: 0 and a very small number
points.body:
The chapter opens by contrasting 0 with a number written as a decimal point followed by 122 zeros and then 138 (about 1.38×10^-123, the cosmological constant in Planck units). The difference looks negligible, yet it may completely change how we imagine reality.

Einstein supposedly called the cosmological constant his "biggest blunder", but the story comes from the hyperbole-prone Gamow and may not be reliable. Either way, general relativity **allows** it, and whether it is zero is for observation to decide.

points.h: Measuring distance: standard candles
points.body:
In 1998, Perlmutter's Supernova Cosmology Project and Schmidt's High-Z Supernova Search Team set out to measure **how quickly the expansion of the universe is slowing down**. The plan: measure the expansion rate at different times in the past and compare.

The first step is distance. **Parallax** (close one eye, then the other, and your finger jumps) works only within a few thousand light-years. Farther out you rely on brightness: the farther, the dimmer. The difficulty is not knowing how bright an object really is. **Type Ia supernovae** are ideal "standard candles": bright enough to be seen at enormous distances, and of essentially uniform intrinsic brightness.

points.h: The cosmic map and its legend
points.body:
How should we think of "distance" in an expanding universe? Greene suggests imagining **an unchanging map of the cosmos**, with the expansion shown only by the **scale in the legend** being updated constantly. If the Earth swelled uniformly to twice its size, a map of the United States would still work; you would just change the scale.

While light is in transit, the stretches it has already crossed keep on being stretched. So comparing a supernova's apparent brightness with its intrinsic brightness gives the galaxy's distance from us **now**.

points.h: Redshift: the universe's height chart
points.body:
A neon sign glows red because electron transitions in neon atoms release photons of specific wavelengths; each element has its own "spectral fingerprint". The fingerprints of distant objects are shifted as a whole toward the red end: **redshift**. The cause is the expansion of space stretching light waves.

If wavelengths are stretched by 3%, the universe is 3% larger than when the light was emitted. Like the pencil marks on a wall recording a child's height: each mark records the size at one moment. You also need to fix the **date** of each mark, taking into account that light both travels through space and is carried along by it, like walking on an airport moving walkway.

points.h: The universe is accelerating
points.body:
After checking, rechecking and checking again, both teams concluded: **for the past seven billion years or so, the expansion of the universe has not been slowing but speeding up.** It had been slowing before, then switched to acceleration about seven billion years ago.

It is as if a ball thrown upward went faster and faster: something must be pushing it. That is exactly the cosmological constant's "job description". The data give a value of less than 10^-29 grams per cubic centimeter. Early on it was overwhelmed by the gravity of ordinary matter; as expansion diluted the matter, it finally gained the upper hand.

The consequence: distant galaxies will be pulled away ever farther and faster, and future astronomers will not be able to see them. For many researchers, this was the **most unexpected observational result** of their lives.

points.h: Theory got it wrong by 123 orders of magnitude
points.body:
Greene's first reaction, like most physicists', was: "Impossible."

Quantum jitters fill even empty space with energy. A direct calculation gives **infinity**; cutting off jitters smaller than the Planck length still leaves about **10^94 grams per cubic centimeter**, denser than all the stars of all known galaxies packed into a thimble. That is off from the observed value by about **123 orders of magnitude**.

Physicists had **hoped** it would be exactly zero, thanks to **symmetry**. Archie has homework: add up the 63rd powers of 1 through 10, then add the sum of the 63rd powers of -1 through -10. He slogs away at it, when one glance shows that the positives and negatives cancel exactly and the answer is 0. **Supersymmetry** could have cancelled things this way, with each particle and its superpartner contributing opposite amounts. Unfortunately that requires the partners to have equal masses, which experiments have ruled out.

points.h: Weinberg's bold prediction
points.body:
In 1987, more than a decade before the supernova observations, Nobel laureate **Steven Weinberg** took a different route and calculated that the cosmological constant should be **small but not zero**. His weapon was **anthropic reasoning**.

Copernicus started a chain of "demotions": we are not at the center of the solar system, nor of the galaxy, nor of the universe, and even the matter we are made of is a cosmic minority. In 1973, at a conference in Kraków honoring Copernicus, **Brandon Carter** proposed a twist: in one respect we really are indispensable, namely that **we observe an environment suited to our existence**.

points.h: The anthropic principle: studying trout in the Sahara
points.body:
If you survey only the Sahara for trout, you will ask "why are trout extinct?" **A biased sample makes you explain things that need no explanation.**

Kepler wanted a deep law to explain why the Earth is 93 million miles from the Sun. Gravity allows any orbital distance; but there are countless planets at all sorts of distances, and we **could only** turn up on one with a suitable temperature. There is no fundamental reason, only historical accident plus an observer selection effect.

No one objects to this part of Carter's idea. The controversy is in extending it to **the universe itself**: if there is a multiverse whose universes have widely varying constants, then asking "why does the electron have this mass?" is asking the wrong question; we are simply in one that allows life.

This takes three assumptions: (1) a multiverse exists; (2) the constants vary over a wide range across universes; (3) most values do not allow life.

points.h: The cosmological constant and galaxies
points.body:
Many constants could not change much without making life impossible: slightly stronger gravity and stars burn out too fast; slightly weaker and galaxies cannot assemble; slightly stronger electromagnetism and hydrogen cannot fuse.

Weinberg swapped in a more tractable question: not whether life exists, but **whether galaxies can form**. Galaxies assemble through gravity's snowball effect, and too large a cosmological constant would push matter apart before the clumping finished. He calculated an upper limit of a few hundred times the density of matter. This was the first theoretical estimate that was not wildly off.

But it requires a multiverse in which **at least one** universe happens to have the value we observe. A casting analogy: to find the lead for producer Harvey W. Einstein's new film *Pulp Friction*, with a height between 1 and 2 meters specified to the centimeter, you need at least a hundred actors, more allowing for duplicates. For a cosmological constant between 0 and 1 specified to 10^-124, you need **far more than 10^124 universes**.

points.h: From vice to virtue: the string landscape
points.body:
Where to find so many universes? In the previous chapter's **10^500 forms of the extra dimensions**. Each form's flux carries a different energy, and so a different cosmological constant. With 10^500 marks scattered between 0 and 1, many are bound to fall near the observed value. "**This is just what the doctor ordered.**"

For those holding on to Einstein's dream of a unique universe, this used to be discouraging. But from the cosmological constant's point of view, string theory suddenly made the least credible part of Weinberg's argument (the need for a vast number of universes) credible.

points.h: The last step: quantum tunneling
points.body:
Greene first gives a three-sentence summary: the inflationary multiverse has an ever-growing number of bubble universes; eternal inflation scatters string theory's 10^500 forms of the extra dimensions across those bubbles, one form per bubble; so all the universes we need are there.

In more detail: upgrade the "mountain" of Chapter 3 into the **string landscape**: many valleys, each a form of the extra dimensions, with altitude representing the value of the cosmological constant. (Strictly it is a landscape of about 500 dimensions, impossible to draw.)

**Quantum tunneling**: an electron meets a ten-foot-thick steel wall that classical physics says it cannot pass, but quantum mechanics says it has a small chance of simply appearing on the other side. Coleman and De Luccia extended this to the whole universe: a "seed" appears somewhere in space, the field value tunnels to a lower valley, and a new bubble forms and expands rapidly. New bubbles can form inside bubbles, nested layer upon layer. This is the **Landscape Multiverse**: a more elaborate Swiss cheese, each of whose holes has different extra dimensions, particles and cosmological constant.

points.h: What about the other constants? Is this still science?
points.body:
Besides the cosmological constant there are the three neutrinos, the electron's mass, the strength of the weak force and more. To make this account credible, one would at least have to show that the landscape **really does contain** a bubble matching our universe in every detail. That is the aim of "string model building", but the landscape is so large and complex that a systematic search is nearly impossible: even analyzing one form per second, a billion years would cover only a tiny fraction.

This chapter takes a logical turn: earlier parallel universes merely **broadened our view of what is out there**; the Landscape Multiverse **directly invokes** worlds we may never see, test or influence in order to explain observations here. So: **is this still science?** (Chapter 7)

expressions.zh: (On getting an infinite answer) nobody had a fit. *Apoplexy* originally means a stroke; *fits of apoplexy* are bouts of rage.

expressions.en: far larger than what you’d get from compressing all the stars in all the known galaxies into a thimble
expressions.zh: An image of unimaginable density.

expressions.zh: *With a vengeance* means forcefully, to an extreme degree. Humanity's demotion keeps going.

expressions.zh: (Surveying only the Sahara) why are trout extinct? (Surveying only outside an opera house) why is public interest in opera surging? Absurd questions to illustrate sampling bias.

expressions.zh: The anthropic principle is an "unfortunate name" because it applies to any intelligent observer, not just humans.

expressions.zh: Greene's invented "notorious" producer and his new film, spoofing Hollywood celebrities and *Pulp Fiction*.
